newsitem.title: USA: Helmsley to sell portfolio, but not hotel crown.
newsitem.headline: Helmsley to sell portfolio, but not hotel crown.

text.p: Leona Helmsley may have put a "for sale" sign on her $5 billion real estate portfolio on Wednesday, but insiders predicted she would cling for dear life to enough hotels to remain in the New York limelight.

"She will keep the best hotels to have something to play with. They're her glamour vehicle. Without them she's just a fabulously rich New Yorker, no longer a queen," said one longtime associate of the controversial heiress.

Eastdil Realty of New York, which specialises in sales to institutional investors, said it had been entrusted to sell the nationwide realm of skyscrapers, apartment buildings, shopping centres and hotels.

Eastdil Chairman Ben Lambert said he would not list any specific building for a few months, until valuations could be made. And he refused to reveal which buildings, if any, Helmsley might want to retain.
"But you can expect her to remain very much involved in the hotel business. She has a real passion for the business," he said.
Would-be buyers for other properties can expect long and tough bargaining from a woman known for going to astounding lengths to save a dollar, former associates said.

Indeed, she served 18 months in federal prison after being convicted of evading about $1 million in taxes -- representing a smidgen of her vast wealth -- by charging off personal purchases as business expenses.

"She'll play one bidder off another. They'll need backbones of steel," one former Helmsley colleague predicted. "Believe me, this won't be a fire sale. She won't part easily with anything because she has an insatiable appetite for money."

Helmsley inherited her portfolio in January upon the death of her husband Harry, the legendary Quaker tycoon who scooped up many of New York's most valuable skyscrapers for a pittance during the years immediately after World War II.

But unlike Harry, a management wizard whose photographic memory kept strict account of office expenses right down to the cost of light bulbs, Mrs. Helmsley has had little direct involvement in most commercial properties.
"She's 76 years old, with no experience in anything but hotels, so selling everything else is the sensible thing to do," said another longterm associate.

He predicted it might take her years to unload her properties, which include the gold-leafed Helmsley Building straddling Park Avenue, the Graybar and Lincoln office buildings near Grand Central Station and properties in Illinois and California.
"She doesn't own many of the properties outright. It's very complex because there are partners she will have to deal with," he added.
All told, the portfolio encompasses 25 million square feet of office space and 20,000 residential units.

Helmsley owns outright the nationwide Harley Hotel chain and her two prized New York City hotels: the New York Helmsley on 42nd Street and the stately Park Lane Hotel opposite Central Park -- whose sprawling penthouse she calls home.
"The Park Lane may not be included in the sale. She likes that hotel because Harry built it," said Helmsley spokesman Howard Rubenstein.
Helmsley's nitpicking perfectionism is often highlighted in advertisements for her hotels, but her crown-topped visage has not appeared since her conviction in 1989.

Although the ads will keep her in the spotlight, as a felon she is prevented by state law from having a direct management role in any hotels which sell alcohol -- including the Park Lane and New York Helmsley.
